newsitem.title: CHINA: China frees Hong Kong reporter Xi Yang on parole.
newsitem.headline: China frees Hong Kong reporter Xi Yang on parole.

text.p: Hong Kong journalist Xi Yang, jailed by China in 1994 for 12 years for stealing state secrets, was released on parole on Saturday and left for the British colony, the official Xinhua news agency said.
The China-born Xi, a former reporter for Hong Kong's Chinese-language Ming Pao newspaper, was released with 157 days to go before the British colony reverts to Chinese rule on July 1, 1997.
He left Beijing for Hong Kong on Saturday evening, Xinhua said.
Xi was paroled because he "showed signs of repentance", the agency said. It gave no further details.

China arrested Xi in 1993 and sentenced him to 12 years in prison the following year for stealing state secrets about internal policies on interest rates and gold, triggering a chorus of protests in the British colony.
The severity of the sentence shocked Hong Kong reporters, already pessimistic about the prospects for a free press after the handover.

His conviction had been seen as an attempt by Beijing to intimidate Hong Kong media before 1997 and to stop reporters from the colony uncovering news not published in the official Chinese media which serves as a tool of the Communist Party.
A clerk at China's central bank, Tian Ye, was jailed for 15 years for giving Xi information on Beijing's interest rate policy and plans for gold sales on the international market.

Diplomats in Beijing welcomed Xi's release but were baffled because China has been tightening its grip on the media, calling on reporters to back the Communist Party's policies and give priority to "positive" reporting.
Separately, China and Hong Kong's outgoing colonial masters, Britain, are embroiled in a row over Beijing's plans to roll back civil liberties in Hong Kong after the handover.
At the time of Xi's sentencing, the United States criticised China, saying the case raised serious questions about whether his secret trial had been fair and the charges against him valid.
Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten attacked the sentence as wholly disproportionate but admitted that there was little he can do for Xi who remains a Chinese citizen.
